items.followUp: Write the chemical formula of aluminium oxide using the valencies of aluminium and oxygen.

rubric.why: The first step is to write the symbols of the elements or ions.
rubric.description: Writes the correct symbols for the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing Mg and Cl.

rubric.why: The valencies are needed before forming the formula.
rubric.description: Writes the valencies of magnesium and chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Mg valency 2 and Cl valency 1.

rubric.why: Criss-crossing the valencies gives the subscripts in the formula.
rubric.description: Criss-crosses the valencies to obtain MgCl₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct criss-cross result.

rubric.why: Subscripts should be reduced to the simplest whole-number ratio when possible.
rubric.description: States that the subscripts are simplified if they have a common factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the simplification rule.

modelAnswer: Step 1: Write the symbols of the elements: Mg and Cl.
Step 2: Write their valencies: Mg = 2 and Cl = 1.
Step 3: Criss-cross the valencies to write them as subscripts: Mg₁Cl₂.
Step 4: Remove the subscript 1; the formula is MgCl₂. Simplify subscripts to the lowest whole-number ratio when possible.

items.followUp: Define a polar covalent bond and give one example of a covalent compound.

rubric.why: Sharing of electron pairs is the defining feature of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent compound as one formed by sharing electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Many covalent compounds have relatively weak forces between their molecules.
rubric.description: States that they generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both low melting and boiling points.

rubric.why: They generally do not have mobile charged particles to carry current.
rubric.description: States that they are generally poor conductors of electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electrical-conduction property.

rubric.why: Their solubility differs from that of many ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States a typical solubility property: soluble in organic solvents or generally insoluble in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either accepted solubility statement.

rubric.why: Many covalent substances occur in these physical forms at room temperature.
rubric.description: States that they are often gases, liquids, or soft solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the physical-state property.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds are formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
They generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
Many are soluble in organic solvents and are generally insoluble in water.
At room temperature, many are gases or liquids; solid covalent compounds are often soft.

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain how temperature and the nature of a liquid affect it.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure is defined for vapour in equilibrium with its liquid.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including equilibrium.

rubric.why: At higher temperature, more liquid particles escape into the vapour phase.
rubric.description: Explains that vapour pressure increases with temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the temperature effect.

rubric.why: The strength of attraction between liquid particles affects how readily they evaporate.
rubric.description: Relates the nature of the liquid and its intermolecular forces to vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct comparison.

rubric.why: A non-volatile dissolved substance reduces the tendency of liquid particles to escape.
rubric.description: States that a non-volatile dissolved solute or impurity lowers vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this factor and its effect.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.
Increasing the temperature increases the vapour pressure.
A liquid with weaker intermolecular forces has a higher vapour pressure because its particles escape more readily.
A non-volatile dissolved solute or impurity lowers the vapour pressure of a liquid.

items.followUp: What is studied in organic chemistry, and how does this differ from inorganic chemistry?

rubric.why: Organic chemistry is identified by the class of compounds it studies.
rubric.description: States that organic chemistry deals mainly with carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct distinction.

rubric.why: Inorganic chemistry covers the remaining elements and compounds, with some carbon compounds treated as inorganic.
rubric.description: Distinguishes inorganic chemistry from organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it deals with other elements and their compounds, or noting that compounds such as carbon dioxide and carbonates are inorganic.

modelAnswer: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals mainly with carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry deals with the other elements and their compounds; some carbon compounds, such as carbon dioxide and carbonates, are also inorganic.

items.followUp: Define one atomic mass unit and state one reason for using it.

rubric.why: The atomic mass unit is defined using one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: Defines 1 u as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Atomic masses are extremely small in ordinary mass units, so a convenient scale is needed.
rubric.description: Explains that the unit makes atomic masses convenient to express and compare.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid reason.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (1 u) is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
It is needed because the actual masses of atoms are extremely small and inconvenient to express in grams or kilograms.

items.followUp: Define relative atomic mass and state the gram mass of one mole of atoms whose relative atomic mass is 23.

rubric.why: Relative atomic mass compares an atom's average mass with the carbon-12 standard.
rubric.description: Defines relative atomic mass using one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct comparison.

rubric.why: The relative atomic mass is numerically equal to the mass in grams of one mole of the element's atoms.
rubric.description: Relates relative atomic mass to gram atomic mass or the mass of one mole in grams.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the numerical relation, with an appropriate example if given.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
It has no unit; its numerical value is equal to the mass in grams of one mole of the atoms (the gram atomic mass).

items.followUp: Differentiate between an energy shell and a subshell, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: A shell is a main energy level around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Defines a shell and gives a suitable example or notation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition with an example such as K shell or n = 1.

rubric.why: A subshell is a subdivision of a shell, designated by letters such as s, p, d, and f.
rubric.description: Defines a subshell and gives a suitable example or notation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition with an example such as 2s or 2p.

modelAnswer: A shell is a main energy level of an atom, represented by n = 1, 2, 3, … or by K, L, M, …; for example, K is the first shell.
A subshell is a subdivision of a shell, represented by s, p, d, or f; for example, the second shell contains 2s and 2p subshells.

items.followUp: Why does atomic radius generally decrease across a period, and why is the decrease not perfectly regular?

rubric.why: Across a period, added electrons enter the same main shell while nuclear charge increases.
rubric.description: States that electrons are added to the same shell across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the same-shell addition.

rubric.why: Changes in nuclear attraction, shielding, and electron repulsion mean the attraction does not change uniformly.
rubric.description: Explains that changing shielding, subshell effects, or electron repulsion makes the size decrease irregularly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant explanation of the irregularity.

modelAnswer: Across a period, electrons are added to the same main shell while the nuclear charge increases, so the atomic size generally decreases.
The decrease is not perfectly regular because shielding, electron–electron repulsion, and subshell effects do not change uniformly.
